# Unit 3 week 4 — Explained answers
A: bubble passes [2,4,1,5], [2,1,4,5], [1,2,4,5]; key comparisons 3,2,1 (6 total). Already sorted n>=1: n-1 comparisons, no swaps, early stop. Reset swapped inside the outer loop.
B: insertion passes [2,5,4,1], [2,4,5,1], [1,2,4,5]; comparisons 1,2,3 (6 total). Save key before shifts; check position>=0 before access. Sorted n-1; reverse distinct n(n-1)/2.
C: selection passes all [1,2,4,5]; comparisons 3,2,1 (6 total), only one swap for this input. Track an index and swap after the minimum scan. Expected outputs: [], [7], [1,2,3], [1,2,3], [1,2,2], [4,4,4], [-2,-1,3]. All three mutate the supplied list and return a key-comparison count. Output order alone does not show preservation; compare to sorted(original) or duplicate frequencies.
D: sorted bubble/insertion counts 7,15,31; selection sorted/reverse and bubble/insertion reverse counts 28,120,496. Best time O(n),O(n),O(n²); worst all O(n²). Routines O(1) extra space; caller copy O(n). Bubble/insertion stable under the strict movement rules; selection on labelled records produces [(1,C),(2,B),(2,A)], reversing equal-key order. Small/nearly sorted can favour insertion; selection bounds swaps by n-1 when stability is unnecessary, but remains quadratic in comparisons. Algorithm choice must name requirements, not promise universal fastest performance. Binary returns a sorted-list index; sorting cost must be included in total work.
Review trace consistency, working code, boundary/duplicate evidence and justified choices. This is optional practice for checking your understanding.
